title: Amdahl's Law
body:
$\text{speedup} \leq \frac{1}{N+\frac{P}{S}}$

> [!warning] Check this against your course material
> The standard statement is $\text{speedup} \leq \frac{1}{S+\frac{P}{N}}$, with *S* the
> serial fraction, *P* the parallel fraction ($S + P = 1$), and *N* the number of
> processors. Your line has *N* and *S* swapped into each other's places. Sanity check: at
> $N = 1$ the formula must give a speedup of exactly 1, since one processor is no speedup
> at all. The standard form gives $\frac{1}{S+P} = \frac{1}{1} = 1$. The line above gives
> $\frac{1}{1 + \frac{P}{S}}$, which is less than 1 for any non-zero *P*, so it claims one
> processor makes the program slower than itself. Your line is left as you wrote it; say
> the word and it changes.

Adding cores does not make a program faster in proportion, because part of it cannot be run
in parallel at all. That part sets a ceiling, and no amount of hardware gets you past it.

**The serial fraction is the [[Critical Section]].** That is the connection this course
cares about: the code that must be serialized is precisely the code that
[[Synchronization]] forces one thread through at a time, so every lock you add raises *S*
and lowers the ceiling.

## The ceiling

Let $N \to \infty$ and the parallel term vanishes, leaving $\text{speedup} \leq
\frac{1}{S}$. Some numbers:

| Serial fraction *S* | Best possible speedup, unlimited cores |
|---|---|
| 50% | 2× |
| 25% | 4× |
| 10% | 10× |
| 5% | 20× |
| 1% | 100× |

A program that is 10% serial can never get more than 10× faster no matter how many
processors you throw at it. With 8 cores it manages about 4.7×, so you are already wasting
most of the hardware.

## What it means in practice

- Shrinking the critical section is worth more than adding cores. Going from 10% serial to
  5% doubles your ceiling; going from 8 cores to 16 barely moves it.
- Real speedup is worse than the formula says, because the formula ignores the cost of
  [[Context Switching]], lock contention, and cold caches after migration (see
  [[Processor Affinity]]).
- It is the argument against locking a whole data structure when you could lock one bucket
  of it.
